text: Features get computed in one place for training and another for predictions, and the copies drift apart. That mismatch is called training-serving skew, and the SageMaker Feature Store exists to prevent it.

Four ideas. A feature group is like a table, with a list of features and their types. A record is one row, identified by a record identifier plus an event time that you supply. The online store keeps only the latest record for each identifier, for fast lookups at prediction time. And the offline store keeps every record as history in S3, for exploration, training and batch predictions.

I simulated those two rules locally in pandas, so this is the idea, not the service. The online view keeps the newest record per customer. Then a late record arrives for customer one, with an earlier event time. The offline history grows by one row, but the online value does not change, exactly as the AWS documentation describes.

History earns its keep when you build training data. A customer's churn label was recorded on February tenth. The right feature is the value known on that date, five orders, not today's value of one. An as-of join gives each label the latest feature at or before its date, so nothing from the future leaks into training.

Now the illustrative boto3 code, not run here. Creating a feature group takes the identifier name, the event time name, the feature definitions, and the configuration of the online and offline stores. AWS notes that provisioning an in-memory online store can take ten to fifteen minutes.

Writing and reading go through a separate runtime client. Put record sends a list of feature names and values, all as strings. Get record returns the latest values for an identifier, which your inference code converts back to numbers.
The features are ready and the model is trained. Now let's serve it. Lesson fifteen is real-time endpoints.
